activities.caption: pair each quantity with its role in the split
activities.name: prDialsMatch

config.prompt: A 20 m/s launch at 40° has been split. Match each piece to its role:

pairs.right: the horizontal dial — gravity never touches it
the vertical dial — gravity runs it down 9.8 m/s every second
the glue between the two problems
the choice that splits one speed into two independent dials

config.why: Two independent dials and one shared clock: 'solve the projectile' means solving the vertical problem for times and heights, the horizontal for distances.

activities.anchor: which is precisely why the components can be solved separately
activities.caption: bet first — the top of the flight
activities.name: prApexPredict

config.q: A projectile launched at 30° reaches the top of its flight. Which is true at that instant?
choices: The projectile stops completely for an instant
It still moves at its full horizontal speed — 17.3 m/s for a 20 m/s launch
Its horizontal speed has halved since launch
config.why: It stops RISING — the vertical component is zero for an instant — but nothing removes the horizontal component, and the downward acceleration never pauses.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the tower demonstration's range
activities.name: prTowerEstimate

config.prompt: A ball fired horizontally at 300 m/s from a 45 m tower lands after 3.03 s — same as the dropped ball. Roughly how far away does it land?
config.why: Range = 300 × 3.03 ≈ 909 m — farther, but not later: both balls strike the ground simultaneously.
config.context: Drop time depends only on the vertical problem: t = √(2h/g). No mass appears anywhere.

activities.caption: file the paths — the shape of the path is the geometry of the force
activities.name: prPathBuckets

config.prompt: Match each scenario to the path it traces:

items.label: a horizontal throw, with gravity pulling down throughout
electrons steered by an electric force, as in old cathode-ray tubes
a magnetic force acting sideways on a moving charge
deep space, after the engines cut and no force remains
a ball thrown off a 45 m tower

config.why: A vertical acceleration layered on steady horizontal motion is a quadratic in x — a parabola. A sideways force bends the path into a circle; no force leaves a straight line.

activities.caption: true or false — the 45° rule and its fine print
activities.name: prAngleJudge

statements.s: 45° maximises range on level ground with no air.
statements.why: sin2θ peaks at 2θ = 90° — the textbook rule, for the textbook model.

statements.s: A 30° drive and a 60° lob land together.
statements.why: Complementary angles share range — the lob just takes longer, useful for clearing obstacles.

statements.s: 45° is the best angle for a shot released two metres above the ground.
statements.why: With a launch-height difference (or drag) the optimum drops below 45° — the rule is the ideal model's, not your arm's.

statements.s: A 20° launch reaches about 68% of maximum range.
statements.why: The sensitivity is asymmetric: steep angles near 45° lose little, shallow angles lose it quickly.

activities.anchor: the parabola as the first model, the one whose errors tell you how strong the air is
activities.caption: fill the blanks — what real air does to the parabola
activities.name: prAirCloze

config.text: Drag grows with speed squared and steals horizontal speed continuously: a cricket ball thrown flat out flies farthest at roughly %%0%%°, a raindrop's descent is capped at about %%1%% m/s, and a spread-eagled skydiver's at about %%2%% m/s.
config.hint: One number per blank — two from the falling caps, one from the cricket ball's best angle.

activities.caption: true or false — mirrors and their images
activities.name: opMirrorJudge

statements.s: A plane mirror's image is virtual — the rays do not actually pass through it.
statements.why: Your brain extends the reflected rays backwards; the image is upright, same size, and as far behind the mirror as you are in front.

statements.s: A mirror must be at least half your height to show your whole body.
statements.why: Checkable with a friend and a rangefinder — and it works wherever the mirror hangs.
They reverse front–back. Text reads reversed because YOU turned it around to face the mirror — a coordination trick, not an optical one.

statements.s: A convex mirror's whole job is a shrunk, wide-angle field of view.
statements.why: Diverging rays give small, upright virtual images — the security mirror's design brief.

activities.anchor: Mirror writing is a coordination trick, not an optical one
activities.caption: slide the divider — what the mirror does vs what you did
activities.name: opMirrorCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider between the two halves of the mirror-writing mystery:

before.label: What the optics does
before.text: Reverses front–back — the axis toward the mirror. Stand on the far side of a sheet of glass and your twin finds your left and right unswapped.

after.label: What you did
after.text: Turned the text around to face the mirror — that rotation swaps its sides, so the reflection reads backwards. The turning did it, not the optics.

config.why: Once the front–back reversal is separated from your own rotation, the 'mirror mystery' dissolves.

activities.anchor: spearfishing requires aiming below the fish
activities.caption: fill the blanks — Snell's law in three numbers
activities.name: opSnellCloze

config.text: Light travels at about ⅔ of c in glass, so glass's refractive index is about %%0%%. Entering a denser medium, light bends %%1%% the normal — and a 2 m-deep pool looks about %%2%% m deep, because the floor's image floats up on exit.
config.hint: n = c/v sets the first blank; the apparent depth is the real one divided by n.

activities.anchor: traps light at far shallower angles
activities.caption: place the critical angle for glass-to-air on the scale
activities.name: opCriticalPlace

config.prompt: Total internal reflection needs light to hit the boundary beyond the critical angle. Place it for glass-to-air (degrees):
config.why: arcsin(1/1.5) ≈ 42°. Water's is 48.8°; diamond's is tiny — which is the fire in the stone.
config.context: The internet's backbone is this rule wearing glass: light bouncing down a hair-thin fibre for kilometres.

activities.caption: pair each player in your eye with its job
activities.name: opEyeMatch

pairs.right: does roughly two-thirds of the bending — air-to-fluid is the biggest index jump you own
fine-focuses by changing shape — fat for near, flat for far
eyeball too long — fixed with a diverging lens
power = 1/f in metres — a +2.0 D lens has f = 0.5 m

config.why: Underwater the cornea's air interface vanishes and the eye nearly stops focusing — why swimming is blurry and goggles restore the air gap.

activities.anchor: nobody has ever reached the foot of one
activities.caption: bet first — two people, one shower
activities.name: opRainbowPredict

config.q: You and a friend stand 10 m apart, both facing the same rain shower with the sun behind you. What do you each see?
choices: Exactly the same rainbow — it is one physical arc sitting at a place
Two different rainbows — each observer gets an arc built from their own drops
No rainbow at all — you must stand much closer together
config.why: A rainbow is an ANGLE — about 40 to 42 degrees from the point opposite the sun — built from whatever drops lie along your line of sight. Move, and different drops supply it; each eye gets its own.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the f-stop arithmetic
activities.name: opCameraSpot

config.prompt: One line of this camera answer is wrong — click it:
lines: An f/2 aperture means the aperture diameter is half the focal length.
Halving the f-number doubles the light-gathering area.
Wide open at f/1.8, backgrounds blur; stopped down at f/11, nearly everything is sharp.
Smartphones rebuild depth of field in software, because thin bodies cannot fit large lenses.
config.correction: Halving the f-number QUADRUPLES the light-gathering area — the diameter doubles, and area goes as diameter squared.
config.why: f/2 → f/1.4 doubles the diameter and quadruples the area: exposure stops are area ratios, not diameter ratios.
